standard.title: Features of Asia-Pacific society
standard.description: the significant social, religious, cultural, economic, environmental and/or political features of different groups in the Asian-Pacific society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain the significant social, religious, cultural, economic and political features of ancient and early societies (AC9HH7K09–K11). They understand how to describe a society across multiple dimensions. They have not yet examined these features in Asia-Pacific contexts — the Khmer Empire, feudal Japan under the Shoguns, or Polynesian societies including Māori and Rapa Nui.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the significant social, religious, cultural, economic, environmental and political features of the chosen Asia-Pacific society — describing how these features shaped the way of life of different groups and how social, cultural and political structures organised daily existence.

nodes.label: Social and political organisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the social and political organisation of the chosen Asia-Pacific society — including the roles of different social classes, the distribution of political authority, and how social hierarchies structured daily life.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of the social hierarchy of the chosen society with at least two groups and their roles.
nodes.typical_width: The social and political hierarchy across the chosen society. Examples: the Khmer Empire as depicted through stone carvings and Zhou Daguan's writings — fishing, trading, temple construction; feudal Japan under the shoguns — emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai, workers — and how these classes promoted social and cultural continuity; Polynesian social organisation including the role of the ariki in Māori and Rapa Nui society; Rapa Nui clan structure — the household and extended clan linked through exchange of goods, wives and labour.
wider: For feudal Japan: analyse how the relationship between different social classes — emperor, shogun, daimyo, samurai and workers — promoted social and cultural continuity, examining why the hierarchy was stable over long periods
For Polynesian societies: compare the role of the ariki (chief) in Māori and Rapa Nui societies to examine how similar social structures produced different cultural practices across the Pacific
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the social and political hierarchy of the chosen society is prerequisite to analysing how turning points disrupted it, how power was exercised within it, and what significant individuals achieved against this backdrop. The social structure is the frame for all subsequent analysis.

response_modes.reason: Students often describe social hierarchies as a list of roles without explaining how they are held together — what obligations, dependencies and belief systems maintain the structure. Scaffold the relational logic of the hierarchy.

success_criteria: Names the main social groups in the chosen society and describes their roles and relationships
Explains how the social hierarchy organised access to power, resources or status

nodes.label: Religious and cultural practices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the religious beliefs and cultural practices of the chosen Asia-Pacific society and explain how these shaped social order, cultural identity and political authority.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of at least one religious or cultural practice and its social or political function.
nodes.typical_width: Religious and cultural features in relation to their social function. Examples: bushido — the samurai code of conduct emphasising frugality, loyalty, martial arts mastery and honour — as a cultural system sustaining feudal Japan; Khmer temple construction (Angkor Wat) as a demonstration of the god-king's power; Polynesian cultural practices — tapa cloth, navigational knowledge, oral traditions; the role of stone tools and fishing in Rapa Nui society.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine bushido as a cultural system that simultaneously trained individual warriors and maintained systemic loyalty across the feudal hierarchy
For the Khmer Empire: examine the concept of the 'deva-raja' (god-king) as a religious-political fusion that enabled Khmer kings to mobilise the population for both construction and warfare

response_modes.reason: Religious and cultural practices vary significantly across the three possible Asia-Pacific contexts. Using more than one context (e.g. samurai bushido vs Polynesian ariki traditions vs Khmer god-king ideology) prevents students from generalising from a single case.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contrast between the god-king ideology of the Khmer Empire (religious authority concentrated in the monarch) and the chiefly structures of Polynesian societies (authority distributed through lineage and exchange) offers rich comparative context for understanding how religion and political authority intersect differently across cultures.
success_criteria: Describes at least one religious or cultural practice of the chosen society with historically specific detail
Explains the social or political function of that practice — what it sustained or organised within the society

nodes.label: Economic and environmental features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the economic activities and environmental context of the chosen Asia-Pacific society and explain how these shaped the way of life of different groups.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of at least one economic activity and its relationship to the social or environmental context.
nodes.typical_width: Economic and environmental features across agriculture, trade, resource use and technology. Examples: Khmer fishing, market trading and temple construction labour; the environmental management of feudal Japan — Tokugawa regulations on farming and tree harvesting; Polynesian economic practices — aquaculture in Nauru, agricultural practices in Hawaii, exchange systems in Rapa Nui; Rapa Nui men's fishing and household-clan exchange of goods.
wider: For feudal Japan: examine the Tokugawa Shogunate's attempts to curb deforestation — heavy regulations on farmers, managing tree harvesting, lighter construction techniques — as an example of environmental management as governance

For Polynesian societies: investigate how environmental challenges were overcome on different islands to make settlement possible (aquaculture in Nauru, agriculture in Hawaii) to show how Polynesian societies adapted to diverse Pacific environments

response_modes.reason: Students need to see the link between economic capacity, environmental context and social organisation — e.g. how Khmer water management enabled the agricultural surplus that supported temple construction and a ruling class. Scaffold this causal chain explicitly.

success_criteria: Describes at least one economic activity of the chosen society and explains how it related to the environmental context
Identifies how economic features shaped the roles and experiences of at least one social group
